b: Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder in the general population. It results from deficiency or dysfunction of vWF.
Why both bleeding time and aPTT are prolonged:
Deficient vWF impairs platelet adhesion to collagen → prolonged bleeding time
Deficient vWF reduces Factor VIII levels (because vWF normally carries and protects Factor VIII) → prolonged aPTT
PT is normal because the extrinsic pathway is unaffected

In young infants with severe bleeding manifestations, the differential diagnosis includes severe thrombocytopenia; severe platelet function disorders, such as Bernard-Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia; type 3 (severe) von Willebrand disease; and vitamin K deficiency.

qs.q: What are the characteristic laboratory findings in a patient with von Willebrand's disease?
qs.e: Von Willebrand's disease presents with a deficiency of vWF and factor VIII, leading to prolonged bleeding time (BT) and prolonged partial thromboplastin time (PTT). Platelet count is typically normal.

qs.q: Which plasma fraction is noted to be the only one that consistently contains von Willebrand factor multimers for the treatment of von Willebrand disease?
qs.e: Cryoprecipitate is a source of fibrinogen, factor VIII, and is the only plasma fraction that consistently contains VWF multimers. DDAVP is another treatment option used to increase plasma VWF.

qs.q: Main abnormality in von Willebrand disease?
qs.e: vWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by absent or dysfunctional vWF protein.

qs.q: What is the main abnormality in von Willebrand disease? ---
qs.e: Von Willebrand disease is caused by a quantitative or qualitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor.

o: Normal PT, prolonged APTT, reduced vWF
qs.e: Reduced vWF quantity causes mildly prolonged APTT (low Factor VIII), prolonged bleeding time, and reduced ristocetin cofactor activity.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by quantitative or qualitative defects in vWF, leading to impaired platelet adhesion and reduced Factor VIII. It presents with mucocutaneous bleeding and can be severe in type 3. Early diagnosis guides targeted therapy.

sections.p: Von Willebrand disease (vWD) results from deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (vWF), a multimeric glycoprotein that mediates platelet adhesion and protects Factor VIII. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical bleeding history, prolonged bleeding time, prolonged aPTT, normal PT, and specific vWF assays.
b: vWF activity (ristocetin cofactor, VWF:RCo) measures function
Factor VIII level reflects vWF carrier function

t.b: Quantifies vWF amount; low levels suggest type 1 or 3
Assesses functional activity; low activity with normal antigen indicates type 2
Low levels support vWF deficiency; normal levels suggest isolated Factor VIII deficiency
Prolonged in vWD; normal in isolated platelet count disorders
Prolonged due to low Factor VIII; normal in isolated platelet disorders

sections.p: Severity is staged by vWF:Ag and activity levels and clinical bleeding score. Type 1 is mild/moderate, type 2 subtypes vary, and type 3 is severe with virtually no vWF.
The primary cause is inherited mutation in the VWF gene. Acquired causes include autoimmune antibodies, heparin therapy, and severe liver disease.
Patients present with mucocutaneous bleeding: epistaxis, easy bruising, menorrhagia, and in severe cases, joint or muscle hematomas.
Confirmatory tests include vWF:Ag, VWF:RCo, Factor VIII, and platelet aggregation with ristocetin. In low‑resource settings, a prolonged bleeding time and aPTT with normal PT can raise suspicion.

t.b: Prolonged in vWD; normal in platelet count disorders
Prolonged due to low Factor VIII; normal in isolated platelet disorders
Abnormal in vWD; normal in Bernard‑Soulier syndrome

sections.p: Severe bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, or uncontrolled menorrhagia require urgent care. Complications include anemia, joint damage, and thrombosis with desmopressin therapy.

Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and use targeted therapy. Desmopressin releases stored vWF; antifibrinolytics control mucosal bleeding; plasma or cryoprecipitate supplies vWF and Factor VIII in severe cases.
Regular monitoring of bleeding symptoms, vWF levels, and Factor VIII. Counsel on avoiding NSAIDs, antiplatelet drugs, and high‑dose aspirin. Vaccination against hepatitis B reduces acquired vWD risk.
Platelet function disorders (Bernard‑Soulier), isolated Factor VIII deficiency, and von Willebrand disease type 2N.
Low vWF:Ag can be falsely normal in pregnancy or liver disease; Factor VIII may be normal in type 2B due to normal activity but abnormal aggregation.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, uncontrolled menorrhagia

faq.q: Can vWD be inherited from one parent?
faq.a: Yes, type 1 and 2 are usually autosomal dominant; type 3 is recessive.
Pregnancy increases vWF levels, often improving bleeding, but some women may still bleed.

faq.q: Is there a cure for vWD?
faq.a: No cure, but effective management with desmopressin, antifibrinolytics, or vWF concentrates controls bleeding.
